title: Witness Voice and Narrator Voice in Historical Chronicles

sections.content: You know free indirect discourse (*Ana miró el reloj. ¿Dónde estaba Pedro?*) and *se preguntó dónde* from B2 Unit 17, as well as reported speech (*dijo que*) from B1 Unit 13. Historical essays and chronicles of memory use free indirect discourse to step briefly inside the perspective of past witnesses or a neighbourhood without breaking the narrative flow with quotation marks or *pensaban que*. The third-person past and conditional tenses stay anchored in the narration, while direct questions, exclamations and point-of-view time words signal that the judgement belongs to the witnesses, not the essayist.

sections.title: Reported speech vs free indirect discourse in a chronicle
rows: Direct: Los vecinos preguntaron: «¿Qué quedará ahora de nuestra plaza?»
Quotation marks, present/future tenses and first-person *nuestra*.
Reported: Los vecinos se preguntaron qué quedaría entonces de su plaza.
Explicit reporting verb (*se preguntaron*), *qué* clause, no question marks.
Free indirect: Los vecinos miraban el solar. ¿Qué quedaría ahora de su plaza?
No reporting verb or quotes; conditional (the future seen from the past) with the witness's time word and question.
Analytical narrator: La demolición transformó el trazado comercial del distrito.
Neutral third-person statement belonging to the essayist.

items.spanish: Los antiguos artesanos contemplaban el solar vacío. ¿Quién rememoraría ahora aquellas tardes de taller?
items.english: The former artisans gazed at the empty plot. Who would recall those workshop afternoons now?

items.spanish: La hija leyó la lápida de bronce en silencio. ¡Cuántos años habían pasado desde la última visita!
items.english: The daughter read the bronze gravestone in silence. How many years had passed since the last visit!

items.spanish: El cronista recorrió el archivo cerrado. Mañana mismo tendría que explicar a los vecinos que las cajas habían desaparecido.
items.english: The chronicler walked through the closed archive. Tomorrow he would have to explain to the residents that the boxes had vanished.

items.spanish: Al evocar el viejo mercado, el ensayo distingue entre el dato oficial y la memoria colectiva del barrio.
items.english: In evoking the old market, the essay distinguishes between official data and the neighbourhood's collective memory.

sections.content: Do not mistake a free indirect question or exclamation for the author's own conclusion: check who is looking, remembering or speaking in the preceding sentence. Look for the combination of past or conditional verbs with direct question marks, exclamations or character-centred time words like 'now' and 'tomorrow'.
